plan.topic: Tirzepatide and hair loss: how common shedding was in the trials, why it happens (telogen effluvium after fast weight loss), when it usually starts and grows back, what helps, and when to see a clinician or dermatologist
plan.angle: Same structure. Replace chapter (3) 'Med Sci (Basel) Oct 9, 2026 review' with: 'What do the 2026 reviews add?'. Use Gupta et al., Science Progress 2026 (PMC13100445): tirzepatide 5.4% vs placebo 0.9% in pooled trials, TE as the main pattern, typically reversible with improvement generally within 3–6 months after weight stabilises. Optionally add the Acta Diabetologica Oct 2026 review on trial vs real-world rates. Any observational relative risk gets 'linked to' plus absolute context, and the BMJ cohort is scoped to type 2 diabetes. Use the Med Sci (Basel) paper only if the scriptwriter can confirm it exists, with a working PubMed/MDPI URL, and quote it exactly.
plan.working_title: Tirzepatide Hair Loss: Does It Grow Back?
plan.why:
Last open item in the Lane A queue (median about 158 watch minutes). Hair has proven demand (Instagram 142, YouTube 81 on day 1), the Oct 9 review gives a fresh hook, and it builds the suggested-video cluster with Protein and Strength. | fact-check: The topic is safe, useful and in-lane: Lane A, regrowth angle, red flags and the 'don't stop' line are all good. One problem: I couldn't confirm the 'Med Sci (Basel) systematic review, Oct 9, 2026'. Two targeted searches didn't find it. Don't build a chapter on a source that can't be confirmed. Verified alternatives:
(a) Gupta AK et al., 'GLP-1 therapies and hair loss: a systematic review…', Science Progress, Apr 17, 2026 (PMC13100445). It reports tirzepatide 5.4% vs placebo 0.9% (pooled trial data). It says TE is 'typically reversible with improvements generally observed within 3-6 months following stabilization of weight', with shedding 1.5–3 months after starting or a dose increase. That last point is a timing statement only: no dosing talk.
(b) Acta Diabetologica review, Oct 14, 2026 (Springer, s00592-026-02812-3). It notes that hair loss rates differ between trials and real-world settings.
(c) BMJ cohort (bmjgroup press release). Scope it to type 2 diabetes, say 'linked to', and give the absolute risk.
SURMOUNT-1 alopecia rates per arm vs placebo must be copied from the NEJM supplement or the Zepbound label. Mention the sex difference only if that source states it. Regrowth timing: say 'often within about 3–6 months after weight stabilises', as an average, not a promise. Kidney caveat on protein. Iron/thyroid/vitamin D only as 'ask your doctor about checking'. No supplement promises. Title is fine: 41 chars, drug first, and the first sentence answers it.

scenes.section: How common is hair loss on tirzepatide?
scenes.narration: Start with the official prescribing information for Zepbound, which is tirzepatide for weight management. In its placebo-controlled trials, hair loss was reported by about four to five in every hundred people on tirzepatide, depending on the dose.

visual.stat_label: Hair loss, tirzepatide by dose, label trials

scenes.section: How common is hair loss on tirzepatide?
scenes.narration: On placebo, it was about one in a hundred.

visual.stat_label: Hair loss on placebo, same label trials

scenes.section: How common is hair loss on tirzepatide?
scenes.narration: Make that human. Picture a fitness class of twenty people, all taking tirzepatide. On those numbers, about one of them might report hair loss. The other nineteen wouldn't. And on placebo, it would be closer to one in a hundred.

visual.stock_query: cheerful fitness class of twenty people

scenes.section: How common is hair loss on tirzepatide?
scenes.narration: But look again at that placebo number. It isn't zero. People on no medicine at all shed hair too, from stress, illness, or a hard few months.

visual.stock_query: stressed person at desk, gentle tone

scenes.section: How common is hair loss on tirzepatide?
scenes.narration: So why would a weight-loss medicine affect hair at all? Here's the twist: the leading explanation isn't the drug itself. It's the speed of the weight loss.

scenes.section: How common is hair loss on tirzepatide?
scenes.narration: In the SURMOUNT-one trial, adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, and without diabetes, lost on average between fifteen and about twenty-one percent of their body weight over seventy-two weeks, depending on the dose.

visual.stat_label: Average weight loss, tirzepatide by dose, 72 weeks

scenes.retention_device: Concrete stat sets up the mechanism

scenes.section: How common is hair loss on tirzepatide?
scenes.narration: That's counting everyone who started treatment. On placebo, the average was about three percent.

visual.stat_label: Average weight loss on placebo, 72 weeks

scenes.section: How common is hair loss on tirzepatide?
scenes.narration: That's a lot of change, fast, for a body. And your hair follicles keep a record of it.

scenes.section: Why does hair shed after weight loss?
scenes.narration: Every hair grows from a follicle that cycles through phases. A long growing phase. A short transition. Then a resting phase, after which the old hair falls out.

scenes.section: Why does hair shed after weight loss?
scenes.narration: Normally, about eighty-five percent of the hairs on your scalp are in the growing phase at any one time.

visual.stat_label: Scalp hairs normally in growing phase

scenes.section: Why does hair shed after weight loss?
scenes.narration: That's why the American Academy of Dermatology says shedding about fifty to a hundred hairs a day is normal. You lose them, and you never notice.

scenes.section: Why does hair shed after weight loss?
scenes.narration: But a big shock to the body, like a serious illness, surgery, childbirth, or losing a lot of weight, can push many follicles into the resting phase at the same time.
scenes.on_screen_text: A shock sends follicles to rest

visual.stock_query: many follicles lying down to nap

scenes.section: Why does hair shed after weight loss?
scenes.narration: In fact, the Academy lists losing twenty pounds or more among the common triggers of excess shedding.

scenes.section: Why does hair shed after weight loss?
scenes.narration: Now here's where it gets strange. Nothing falls out right away. Those follicles rest for a few months, then let go together. So the shed seems to come out of nowhere.
scenes.retention_device: 'Here's where it gets strange' re-hook, pays off 'why months later'

scenes.section: Why does hair shed after weight loss?
scenes.narration: And here's a reassuring clue. A hair shed this way often has a tiny pale bulb at the root. That's a resting hair, sometimes called a club hair. It's not a sign the follicle is gone.

visual.stock_query: single hair with pale bulb, magnified

scenes.section: Why does hair shed after weight loss?
scenes.narration: Telogen effluvium doesn't scar the follicle. Therefore, in most cases, the follicle simply starts a new growing phase. A new hair is already on its way.

scenes.section: Why does hair shed after weight loss?
scenes.narration: So does tirzepatide attack hair follicles directly? The review found no human studies showing that. It says tirzepatide was most often linked to telogen effluvium, with rapid weight loss a likely contributor.

visual.fact: No human studies show a direct effect; tirzepatide is most often linked to telogen effluvium

scenes.section: Why does hair shed after weight loss?

scenes.section: When does shedding start and stop?
scenes.narration: Step one: a stretch of fast weight loss. About two to three months after starting treatment, shedding may appear.

visual.stock_query: Dana noticing hair on pillow, calm

scenes.section: When does shedding start and stop?
scenes.narration: Step two: while weight keeps dropping quickly, shedding can carry on. Frustrating, yes, but it fits the biology.

scenes.section: When does shedding start and stop?
scenes.narration: Step three: weight stabilises. Improvement is generally seen within about three to six months after that. That's a typical pattern, not a promise.

scenes.section: When does shedding start and stop?
scenes.narration: Step four: fullness. New hairs start out short, so thickness takes longer to return. The American Academy of Dermatology says most people's hair regains its normal fullness within about six to nine months, once the body readjusts.

scenes.section: What helps tirzepatide hair loss?
scenes.narration: First, and most important: don't stop or change your medicine on your own because of shedding. Bring it to your prescriber. They can weigh it against everything else the medicine is doing for you.

scenes.section: What helps tirzepatide hair loss?
scenes.narration: Second, eat enough. Very low calorie or very low protein eating can trigger shedding by itself. So a quieter appetite shouldn't turn into a crash diet.

scenes.section: What helps tirzepatide hair loss?
scenes.narration: Build meals around a protein source, and add vegetables, fruit and whole grains. Our own tip: eat the protein first, while your appetite is still there.

visual.stock_query: salmon, beans and greens on plate

scenes.section: What helps tirzepatide hair loss?
scenes.narration: If you have kidney disease, ask your doctor how much protein is right for you.

scenes.section: What helps tirzepatide hair loss?
scenes.narration: Third, ask your doctor whether it's worth checking your iron and thyroid. Low iron and thyroid problems can each cause shedding on their own, and both can be treated.
scenes.retention_device: Question to bring to the doctor

scenes.section: What helps tirzepatide hair loss?
scenes.narration: Fourth, be gentle while it sheds. Looser styles, a wide-tooth comb, less high heat. It won't stop a shed, but there's no reason to add strain.

scenes.section: What helps tirzepatide hair loss?
scenes.narration: Now, the fix I promised to explain. Many hair, skin and nail supplements are sold with high doses of biotin.

scenes.section: What helps tirzepatide hair loss?
scenes.narration: The FDA warns that biotin can interfere with certain lab tests and cause incorrect results.

scenes.section: What helps tirzepatide hair loss?
scenes.narration: One of those is troponin, a blood test that helps doctors diagnose heart attacks. The FDA has received reports of biotin causing falsely low troponin results. That's a test you'd want to be accurate.

scenes.section: What helps tirzepatide hair loss?
scenes.narration: The FDA notes that biotin is often found in dietary supplements, and some people don't realise they're taking it. So mention any supplements you take, including hair, skin and nail gummies, to your doctor, especially before blood tests. A two-second conversation solves it.

scenes.section: What helps tirzepatide hair loss?
scenes.narration: And if shedding is really weighing on you, a dermatologist can confirm what kind of hair loss it is and talk you through options that fit you.

scenes.section: What helps tirzepatide hair loss?
scenes.narration: But sometimes, hair loss isn't the usual shed at all. Here's how to tell the difference.

scenes.section: When should you see a doctor?
scenes.narration: Telogen effluvium has a typical look. Thinning spread across the whole scalp, not distinct bald patches.

scenes.section: When should you see a doctor?
scenes.narration: So see a doctor or dermatologist if you notice round or patchy bald spots, or a scalp that's itchy, sore, red or scaly. Those can point to other causes. Or if the thinning is concentrated at your hairline, temples or crown rather than spread out. That can be pattern hair loss, which a dermatologist can assess and treat.

items: Itchy, sore, red or scaly scalp
Thinning at hairline, temples or crown

scenes.section: When should you see a doctor?
scenes.narration: Also check in if heavy shedding lasts longer than about six months. Doctors call that chronic telogen effluvium, and it deserves a proper look for other causes.

scenes.section: When should you see a doctor?
scenes.narration: And if hair loss comes with other changes, like unusual tiredness or feeling generally unwell, mention those too.

scenes.section: When should you see a doctor?
scenes.narration: None of these signs mean something terrible. They mean it's worth a closer look, rather than waiting it out.

factcheck.summary: The science is solid, and the script is safe and well structured. I checked the key numbers against the sources and they match: Gupta 2026 (5.4% [119/2183] vs 0.9% [22/2221]; the exact "typically reversible…3-6 months following stabilization of weight" quote; onset about 2–3 months; "no studies in humans" showing a direct effect on follicles), the Zepbound label (alopecia 5%/4%/5% by dose vs 1% on placebo), SURMOUNT-1 (15.0–20.9% vs 3.1% at 72 weeks), StatPearls (about 85% of hairs in the growing phase, club hairs, non-scarring, chronic after more than 6 months) and the AAD (50–100 hairs a day, losing 20+ lb as a trigger, fullness in 6–9 months). The safety lines and the "don't stop on your own" line are both present. One thing needs fixing before this ships. In s58, and partly s55, the script credits the FDA troponin page with claims it doesn't make: that people may not realise they're taking biotin, and that hair, skin and nail supplements contain it. I checked the page and neither claim is on it. Crediting a source with something it didn't say has caused a hold before (S2 10-24). The other fixes are wording and scope polish.

issues.claim: The FDA notes that biotin is often found in dietary supplements, and some people don't realise they're taking it.
issues.problem: The cited FDA troponin page (21 Jun 2022) says biotin is 'often found in dietary supplements' but says nothing about people not realising they take it. This credits FDA with a claim its page doesn't make.
issues.fix: Replace the narration with: "The FDA notes that biotin is often found in dietary supplements. So mention any supplements you take, including hair, skin and nail gummies, to your doctor, especially before blood tests. A two-second conversation solves it."

issues.claim: Many hair, skin and nail supplements are sold with high doses of biotin. (source: fda_biotin)
issues.problem: The cited FDA troponin page never mentions hair, skin or nail supplements. Its only wording is 'often found in dietary supplements'. The source tag doesn't support the line.
issues.fix: Replace the narration with: "Now, the fix I promised to explain. Biotin. It's a vitamin that's often found in dietary supplements, and it's a popular pick for hair." Keep on_screen_text as "The fix: biotin" and keep source_ids ["fda_biotin"].

issues.claim: It says tirzepatide was most often linked to telogen effluvium, with rapid weight loss a likely contributor.
issues.problem: The review says tirzepatide is 'particularly associated with TE'. 'Most often' is a slightly stronger, quantitative paraphrase. The myth_fact card repeats it.
issues.fix: Change the narration to: "It says tirzepatide was particularly linked to telogen effluvium, with rapid weight loss a likely contributor." Change on_screen_text to "Tirzepatide: particularly linked to telogen effluvium" and the myth_fact fact to "No human studies show a direct effect; tirzepatide is particularly linked to telogen effluvium". In s04, change "the pattern reviewers link it to most often" to "the pattern reviewers link it to".

issues.claim: Picture a fitness class of twenty people… about one of them might report hair loss… And on placebo, it would be closer to one in a hundred.
issues.problem: The class-of-20 frame mixes awkwardly with 'one in a hundred'. It also leaves out a label fact that matters to this audience and to Dana: hair loss was reported more often in women (7.1%) than in men (0.5%) on tirzepatide.
issues.fix: Change the narration to: "Make that human. Picture a fitness class of twenty people, all taking tirzepatide. On those numbers, about one of them might report hair loss. The other nineteen wouldn't. One more detail from the label: it was reported more often in women than in men." Add an on-screen line, "Reported more often in women (label)", with source_ids ["zepbound_label"].

issues.claim: The leading explanation isn't the drug itself. It's the speed of the weight loss.
issues.problem: The review says no human studies show a direct effect on follicles and names rapid weight loss as a contributor. 'Isn't the drug itself' sounds more settled than that.
issues.fix: Change the narration to: "So why would a weight-loss medicine affect hair at all? Here's the twist: there's no human evidence the drug acts on hair directly. The leading explanation is the speed of the weight loss."

issues.claim: That's why the American Academy of Dermatology says shedding about fifty to a hundred hairs a day is normal.
issues.problem: 'That's why' links the 85% growing-phase figure to the AAD's number as cause and effect. The AAD doesn't make that link.
issues.fix: Change the narration to: "And the American Academy of Dermatology says shedding about fifty to a hundred hairs a day is normal. You lose them, and you never notice."

issues.claim: The American Academy of Dermatology says most people's hair regains its normal fullness within about six to nine months
issues.problem: The AAD says hair 'tends to' regain its normal fullness within six to nine months. 'Most people's' adds a proportion the source doesn't give.
issues.fix: Change to: "The American Academy of Dermatology says that once the body readjusts, hair tends to regain its normal fullness within about six to nine months."
